sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); the linked copy was not accessible when a reader tried
sources.note: The only publication with first-hand Inku data (a Vangawala text, pp. 85ff., and remarks on the four varieties, p. 82). Needs to be read to confirm whether it has any phonological or stress remark; second-hand (Wikipedia citing p. 82) says the materials are unpublished and unanalysed, so a stress statement is unlikely but this is the one place it could be.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1994. Peripatetics of Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey. In John Middleton & Amal Rassam (eds.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, vol. IX: Africa and the Middle East, 274-276. Boston: G. K. Hall. (Glottolog ref 326078; read in the encyclopedia.com reprint.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'within each group, a separate dialect or language is spoken. The latter are either of Indic or Iranian origin, and many are structured somewhat like an argot or secret language' - nothing on stress

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1992. "Jat." In Paul Hockings (ed.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, Vol. 3: South Asia, 110-113. Boston: G.K. Hall. (Read in the encyclopedia.com transcription.)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology, stress or tone; the linguistic paragraph is generic and concerns scripts (Urdu/Gurmukhi/Devanagari) used by South Asian Jats.

sources.citation: Kieffer, Charles M. 1983. "Afghanistan v. Languages." Encyclopaedia Iranica I/5, pp. 501-516 (online edition, iranicaonline.org).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing about Inku stress. Sections 19-22: "other Indian minority groups speak Sindhī (20) and Inku (Lahndā, 22).. Dialects of the Sirāikī (Sindkhī) type, about which relatively little is known, are used by the Vaṛŋgāwālā, the Pikrāǰ, the Šādībāz, and the Jalālī"; section 32: Rao's Jat materials "will be published in collaboration with Ch. M. Kieffer" (no such publication located). The article's only stress remark concerns Dari, not Inku. downloaded from the Internet Archive copy (2023-11-17) because iranicaonline.org could not be reached by automated download.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna (with Ch. M. Kieffer, announced). Unpublished field materials on the languages of the Jat (Vangawala, Pikraj, Shadibaz, Jalali) collected in Afghanistan in the 1970s; announced in Kieffer 1983, Encyclopaedia Iranica "Afghanistan v. Languages", section 32 as "will be published in collaboration with Ch. M. Kieffer".

sources.note: The only primary linguistic corpus of Inku known to exist; never published as far as any bibliography shows (Rao died 2005). If it survives in an archive it is the only possible basis for a phonological statement.
